title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time the way people really say it, name the days and months, and place events in yesterday, today or tomorrow.
bekal: read the clock with *alas-* and add the part of day (*ng umaga*, *ng gabi*)
name the seven days and twelve months — all from Spanish

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Anong oras ang klase?
dialogs.intro: Budi has just signed up for a course. Mia explains the schedule while typing it into her phone.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Alas-otso ng umaga. Huwag kang ma-late!
lines.id: Eight in the morning. Don't be late!
lines.literal: o'clock-eight of morning. don't you be-late!

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Hanggang alas-onse lang naman. May pahinga sa alas-nuwebe y medya.
lines.id: Only until eleven. There's a break at half past nine.
lines.literal: until o'clock-eleven only indeed. there-is rest at o'clock-nine and half.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Okay. What days is the class?

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Wala. Pero may practice tayo sa Sabado ng hapon.
lines.id: No. But we have practice on Saturday afternoon.
lines.literal: none. but there-is practice we on Saturday of afternoon.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Ika-labinlima ng Hunyo. Mag-eexam tayo sa katapusan ng buwan.
lines.id: The fifteenth of June. We have an exam at the end of the month.
lines.literal: 15th of June. will-have-exam we at end of month.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Oh no! I need to start studying.

notes: **Time uses Spanish numbers, always.** *Alas-otso* (8 o'clock), *alas-dos* (2 o'clock), *alas-singko* (5 o'clock). The only exception is one o'clock: *ala-una*, with *ala-* not *alas-*, because in Spanish "one o'clock" is singular.
**The part of the day is added with ng.** *Alas-otso ng umaga* (8 a.m.), *alas-otso ng gabi* (8 p.m.). Without this, a time in the Philippines can mean two different times twelve hours apart.
**Y medya means half** (from Spanish *y media*): *alas-nuwebe y medya* = half past nine, literally "nine o'clock and a half". Same logic as English "half past", with no "half to" trick.

**Ika- is the formal form.** *Ika-walo ng umaga* equals *alas-otso ng umaga*, but is used in invitations, official schedules and news. For dates, though, *ika-* is the usual one: *ika-labinlima ng Hunyo*.
**Ang aga naman** uses the unit 3 exclamation pattern with the root *aga* (early morning). Its cousins: *ang gabi na* (it's already so late), *ang tagal* (so long).
**Hanggang means "until"** — used for time and place alike: *hanggang alas-onse*, *hanggang Maynila*. It's also used when parting: *hanggang bukas* (until tomorrow).

**Ma-late is perfect Taglish**: the Tagalog prefix *ma-* attached to the English word *late*. The pattern is alive and productive — *mag-shopping*, *nag-jogging*, *ma-stress*. You'll hear it often, and nobody thinks it's wrong.
**Naku!** is an all-purpose exclamation: surprise, disappointment, dismay, exasperation. Longer form *ay naku*, and a stronger one *naku po*. The closest English matches: "oh my!" or "oh no!"
**Katapusan ng buwan** = end of the month. The word *katapusan* also means "end" in general, from the root *tapos* (finished). A nice reminder that one root can generate a whole family of words.

grammars.title: Reading the clock
body: The standard question is *Anong oras na?* and the standard answer uses *alas-* + a Spanish number.
after: The parts of day you can attach: *ng umaga* (morning, 6-11), *ng tanghali* (midday, 11-1), *ng hapon* (afternoon, 1-6), *ng gabi* (night, 6-12), *ng madaling-araw* (before dawn, 1-5).
To ask what time something happens: *Anong oras ang klase?* To answer when, add *sa*: *Sa alas-otso.*
Times that aren't round are often said in English: *eight forty-five*. That isn't laziness but habit — even native speakers do it.

grammars.title: Days, months and time words
body: The names of the days and months all come from Spanish, so none of them needs guessing.
after: *Linggo* does two jobs: Sunday **and** one week. *Sa Linggo* = on Sunday; *isang linggo* = one week. Context separates them, and native speakers are never confused.
Days always begin with *sa*: *sa Lunes* (on Monday). For habitual repetition use *tuwing*: *tuwing Lunes* (every Monday).
Dates are written with *ika-*: *ika-lima ng Mayo* (May 5). In fast speech, people often switch straight to English: *May five*.

blocks.text: Notice two opposing prefixes: **ka-** points backward (*kahapon*, *kagabi*, *kanina*), while **sa** points forward (*sa makalawa*, *sa Linggo*, *sa susunod*). Once you see this pattern, half the words in this table don't need to be memorized one by one.

blocks.title: Noong and sa
items: **Noong** marks past time: *noong Lunes* (last Monday), *noong 2020*, *noong bata pa ako* (when I was little).
**Sa** marks future time: *sa Lunes* (next Monday), *sa Disyembre*, *sa susunod na taon*.
These two small words replace the whole tense system that Tagalog doesn't have — and that's why Tagalog verbs don't need to mark time themselves.

blocks.text: *Gaano katagal* asks for duration, and the answer uses ordinary time units: *limang minuto*, *dalawang oras*, *tatlong araw*, *isang linggo*, *anim na buwan*, *isang taon*.

exercises.prompt: Write the following times in Tagalog.
Fill in the right time word: kahapon, bukas, kanina, mamaya, ngayon, kagabi.
items: Natulog ako nang maaga ____. (the night just past)
Kumain kami sa labas ____. (one day before today)
Tawagan mo ako ____. (in a few hours)
The class is at eight in the morning.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: linggo / sa / darating / susunod / na / siya

answers: alas-otso ng umaga — ala-una ng hapon — alas-siyete y medya ng gabi — alas-diyes kinse ng umaga — hatinggabi — alas-singko ng umaga
kanina — bukas — kagabi — ngayon — kahapon — mamaya
Anong oras na? — Anong araw ngayon? — Alas-otso ng umaga ang klase. — Walang klase sa Sabado. — Tuwing Lunes ako nagtatrabaho.
Anong oras na? — Alas-otso ng umaga. — Anong oras ang klase bukas? — Walang klase sa Sabado. — Darating siya sa susunod na linggo.
